nameStory: Little bluestem gets its name from the beautiful blue-green tint that develops in its stems and leaf sheaths, especially during the growing season. The 'little' part distinguishes it from its taller prairie cousin, big bluestem, though both grasses can look quite similar when young.
description: Little bluestem is a clump-forming native grass that grows in neat, upright bunches about 1-3 feet tall. This warm-season perennial is one of New England's most important prairie grasses, with narrow blue-green leaves that turn gorgeous shades of orange, red, and purple in fall. It produces delicate, feathery seed heads in late summer that catch the light beautifully and persist into winter.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms distinct clumps or bunches rather than spreading by runners, with stems growing straight up from a central base in tight clusters

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, flat leaves about 1/8 to 1/4 inch wide with a distinctive blue-green color, especially noticeable at the base where leaf meets stem

idTips.label: Seed Heads
idTips.description: Delicate, branched clusters of tiny seeds with fluffy white hairs that create a feathery appearance and feel soft to the touch

idTips.label: Fall Color
idTips.description: Transforms into brilliant shades of orange, bronze, red, and purple in autumn, making it one of the most colorful grasses in the landscape

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, wiry stems that often develop a blue or purplish tint, especially near the joints where leaves attach

habitat: Look for little bluestem in sunny, well-drained areas like old fields, meadows, roadsides, and rocky slopes throughout New England. It thrives in poor to moderate soils and is often found growing alongside other native grasses, wildflowers like goldenrod and asters, and shrubs in open habitats. This adaptable grass can handle drought well and is common in areas that were once farmed but have been left to return to nature.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as bright green shoots from the base of old clumps, with the distinctive blue-green coloring becoming apparent as leaves mature.
seasonality.summer: Reaches full height with blue-green foliage at its most pronounced, beginning to produce flowering stems in mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Spectacular color show begins as leaves turn brilliant orange, red, and purple, while fluffy seed heads develop and disperse in the wind.
seasonality.winter: Persistent tan and bronze stems and seed heads remain standing, creating winter interest and providing food for birds and small mammals.

funFact: Little bluestem uses a special type of photosynthesis called C4 that makes it incredibly efficient at capturing carbon dioxide in hot weather, which is why it thrives during the hottest summer months when cool-season grasses go dormant!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with big bluestem when young, but little bluestem always grows in tight clumps while big bluestem spreads more and gets much taller (4-6 feet). Memory trick: 'Little stays in a bunch, big spreads out to lunch.'
contextualKnowledge: Though called a 'prairie grass,' little bluestem was actually common in New England's natural grasslands before European settlement and is making a comeback as people restore native plant communities. It's also popular in native plant gardens and sustainable landscaping.
compareHints: Little bluestem is the only member of its genus commonly found in New England, making it unique among our native grasses. It's most similar to other bunchgrasses like poverty grass, but little bluestem is much more robust and develops that characteristic blue-green coloring. Unlike spreading grasses in the same family, little bluestem always maintains its clumping growth habit throughout its life.
